sections.b: In 1 Enoch 85–90 every being is moved one step down the ladder of creation. Humans are animals, angels are "white men," and fallen angels are stars. The righteous line from Adam to Isaac are white cattle; Israel from Jacob on are sheep; the nations are unclean beasts and birds of prey; kings are rams; God is "the Lord of the sheep." Only Noah and Moses "become men" (1 Enoch 89:1, 36). No one is named, so the reader decodes it with the Bible open.

From the exile on, God hands Israel to seventy shepherds, angels who are to punish the flock within limits while another angel writes down every excess (1 Enoch 89:59–64). They rule in four groups of 12, 23, 23 and 12, matching the Babylonian, Persian, Ptolemaic and Seleucid eras. At the end they are judged and thrown into the fire with the fallen stars (1 Enoch 90:25). The idea joins Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11), Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24), the bad shepherds of Ezekiel 34 and Zechariah 11, and the angels set over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8).

After the great horn (Judas Maccabeus) and a final battle, God judges the stars, the shepherds and the blinded sheep, folds up the old house, and brings a new one with no tower (1 Enoch 90:20–29). The nations join the sheep, a white bull is born, and all become white cattle: humanity is made one and righteous again, as at the start (1 Enoch 90:37–38).

common: Most scholars date the Animal Apocalypse to about 164–160 BC, during the Maccabean revolt.
The great horn of 1 Enoch 90:9 is almost always identified with Judas Maccabeus.
uncommon: Some nineteenth-century scholars dated the vision to the reign of John Hyrcanus (134–104 BC).
Daniel Olson argues that the vision's climax is the blessing of all nations promised to Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

sections.b: The Animal Apocalypse reaches its own day in 1 Enoch 90:6–16. Lambs with open eyes are born; the ravens (the Seleucids) kill one (perhaps the high priest Onias III, 2 Maccabees 4:33–38); horns grow, and a great horn sprouts (Judas Maccabeus, 1 Maccabees 3:1–9). The birds of prey gather against it, and an angel comes down to help, as 2 Maccabees 11:6–10 tells of a rider in white near Beth-zur in 164 BC. Then the sheep are given a great sword (1 Enoch 90:19). Unlike Daniel, which calls the fighters "a little help" (Daniel 11:34), Enoch's vision backs the armed revolt.

Enoch tells Methuselah two dreams he saw before he married. The first shows the earth collapsing into the abyss, the Flood, and Enoch prays that a remnant will survive (1 Enoch 83–84). The second, the Animal Apocalypse, shows all history from Adam to the new creation with animals for people (1 Enoch 85–90). In it Enoch is lifted up to watch from a high place (1 Enoch 87:3), the vision's way of reading "God took him" (Genesis 5:24), and Elijah is later brought up to join him (1 Enoch 89:52).

sections.h: Fallen stars in the Animal Apocalypse
sections.b: 1 Enoch 86–88 retells the Watchers story with stars: one star falls first (Asael), then many (Shemihazah's company). They mate with the cows and father elephants, camels and donkeys, the giants, who devour the cattle. Archangels bind the stars hand and foot and throw them into the abyss, and the giants are set against each other. At the last judgment the stars are judged first (1 Enoch 90:24). Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 share the picture of angels bound for judgment.

The Animal Apocalypse turns Jeremiah's seventy years into seventy angelic shepherds who rule Israel from the fall of Jerusalem to the end, in four groups (12, 23, 23, 12). Like Daniel 9:24, it stretches the seventy years over the whole time of foreign rule, and like Zechariah 1:12–15 it says the powers that punished Israel went too far (1 Enoch 89:59–90:25).

1 Enoch 89:59–90:25 assumes that God sets heavenly beings over his people as he set them over the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8). The seventy shepherds are given Israel to rule, betray their trust, and are judged and thrown into the fire, much as Psalm 82 pictures God judging the unjust "gods" and Isaiah 24:21 the host of heaven.

sections.h: A new house with no tower
sections.b: In 1 Enoch 90:28–29 God folds up the old house (Jerusalem) like a tent and brings a new house, larger and higher. The tower that stood for the Temple is not mentioned again, an early parallel to Revelation 21:22, where the city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple. Tobit 14:5 and Ezekiel 40–48, by contrast, expect a rebuilt Temple.

sections.h: The tower and its defiled table
sections.b: In the Animal Apocalypse the Temple is a tower on the house of Jerusalem, where the Lord of the sheep stands (1 Enoch 89:50). It is burned by Babylon (89:66) and rebuilt after the exile, but "all the bread on it was defiled and not pure" (1 Enoch 89:73). The vision rejects the Second Temple's worship from its first day, going further than Malachi 1:7, and the new house at the end has no tower (90:29).

1 Enoch 89:52 has Elijah brought up to Enoch, and 90:31 brings the two back together before the judgment. Early Christian writers, among them Tertullian and Hippolytus, and Ethiopian tradition, identified the two witnesses of Revelation 11 with Enoch and Elijah, the two people the Bible says were taken without dying. Others think of Moses and Elijah, because of the miracles in Revelation 11:6.

At the end of the Animal Apocalypse a white bull with large horns is born, and all creatures fear him and pray to him; then all become white cattle (1 Enoch 90:37–38). He matches Adam, the first white bull (85:3), and is usually called a messianic figure, though he fights no battle and judges no one. Christian readers, including the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, read him as Christ, the second Adam.

In 1 Enoch 83 the boy Enoch dreams of the sky falling and the earth sinking into the abyss, and prays that a remnant will survive. In the Animal Apocalypse the Flood is a roof with seven torrents pouring into an enclosure, and the giants drown (1 Enoch 89:2–8). Enoch's last words remember the first dream (90:42): the Flood is the pattern of the final judgment, as in Matthew 24:37–39 and 2 Peter 3:5–7.

In 1 Enoch 83–84 Enoch prays for the earth before the Flood, and his prayer is answered in Noah. In the Animal Apocalypse he cries out for the sheep (89:57), and the recording angel pleads for them before God (89:76), much as the angel of the LORD asks for mercy on Jerusalem in Zechariah 1:12.
